review_text_raw:
[b][i]Need to Know[/i][/b] is a surveillance simulation, the gameplay of which is somewhat reminiscent of the cold and  calculated [i]papers, please[/i]. You assume the role of an employee of an NSA-like organization called The Department of Liberty, and take care of checking people's browsing history and other personal information to identify a possible security risk. The game gives you more options and scary ways to control the longer you play and rise in security clearance. There is always an elementary question floating in the room: Do you stand up for individual rights or do you help to create an uncontrollable police state.

With its topics, [b][i]Need to Know[/i][/b] is not only closer to reality than many other games, it also creates a completely new game approach that will involve many moral decisions. The gameplay, which is basically just scanning data and making quick decisions, is very close to the border crossing simulation [i]papers, please[/i]. Nevertheless, since then hardly any studios have dared to deal with a political issue that affects us all in a similarly dry and fascinating way.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Memorable characters
- Nice story events
- Wonderful atmosphere
- Highly addictive

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- Won't appeal to everyone
- Takes some trial and error 

[h1]8/10[/h1]

DISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | [b][u]GREAT[/u][/b] | AMAZING | MASTERPIECE

EDIT: I changed from not recommended to recommended. Because the game (tactics) change after reaching clearance level 8. Still the below criticizm is applied, but for a game with this pricetag it doesn't to that bad.

So i was hyped for this game from the start & a early kickstarter funder, but it feels like a disappointment for now.
I specially played this game for a few hours to see if it just has a slow start. But sadly it doesn't only have a slow start.. It keeps slow (might even call it boring). 
Only positive note i have at this moment is, that the story is well written and has some noticable real life scenarios.

Another bad thing (in my opinion) is the time it takes to unlock new ablilities. This only happens when you reach a new/higer clearence level. 
I have more then 4 hours into the game. And i only just unlocked clearance level 8 and therby new abilities. This takes to long in my opinion..

The game has the "beta" feel all over itself. Feels cluncky, UI is horrible to work with & windows get blocked constantly. Rules window should be movable at least.
Crashes at weird moments and nothings happening at the same point after restarting the game.

Also the evidence that needs to be collected, can be very conflicting. The rules states that something needs to be collected. But it it isn't directly linked to your suspect but a contact. The game states that you made a wrong choice.

Just as many i was hoping for a "Papers, Please" like gameplay and challenge, but than in a intelligence styled jacket.
This game is disappointing on all fonts:
- Gets boring soon, game also needs some kind of speed mode.
- Sometimes very unclear/conflicting what kind of evidence needs to be collected.
- You get new ways to check on people but no new tools to use, but only whit new clearance levels.
- Just point and click/memory playstyle. I miss some sort of typing involved (for example keyboard shortcuts), playing as an analist.
- Some times theres logic in "linking" people or suspects together early on. You just/simply can't... This is only possible when the game tells you to.
- (to hide spoilers) You do the same thing anywere.
- Buying stuff.. Ehh, whats the use of this? Whats the use of making money in this game anyway. I don't even have to pay rent.. 
- Weird saving structure. Log out before "End Session" aaaand start all over again with the same mission.
- When you "start over" a session by quitting the game. The location and names of the suspects is the same every time & also their logs.
- Crashes mid game (had three in less than 4 hours of gameplay).

It's just constantly doing the same thing.. Over and over.
This is the thing with most games and isn't that big of an issue. 

The issue with this game is, that there isn't enough variation in "what" to do. 
There is just to little to do to keep it interesting. It's way too late in the game & taking way too long to get there, if you even get there you're interest in this game is most likely already gone.

Still putting all the negative points aside. For their first (major) game, it's actually quite good.
I'm certain they will improve the game and crush some bugs in the oncoming days. So lets see how this plays out!

There's a very good game here, somewhat hidden under a clunky UI. Once you get past some of the unclear instructions, the gameplay is straightforward and can be very enjoyable. You just have to work out the logic behind some of the decisions you're required to make, and that can take one or two do-overs.

I've waited for this game for two years, as have many other people, and I'm choosing to give the devs the benefit of the doubt. Clearly this game is a labour of love and with some tweaks could become a whole lot of fun.

UPDATE 1.02: Just as an addition, the post-launch work that the devs have put in shows that they *are* listening to the community. They are not just fixing bugs but also taking the advice of players to make improvements to gameplay and the UI. This is really good to see.

review_text_raw:
I feel the need to review this now of all times, during the stream of update. Need To Know is fantastic, but it had glaring flaws at launch. I don't believe that this is cause for negative reviews, especially since so many people tend to make a review, and never change it. So here we are.

The game itself is great. Fantastic story, interesting gameplay in the realm of Papers Please/Orwell (Wow bet you've never heard that one before), and compelling decisions, such as the option to weasel your way out of major financial pits by looking at the person who you'd be paying's profile. 

But it was a bit...unclear at first. I spent a lot of time figuring out how to work certain features, as when I first started playing, there had been no updates. No updates, no bug reports, nothing. I was on a 5 hour plane ride, which turned out to be the best time to learn, because I had the time and patience to do it. Once I hit ground, there was already a post about the upcoming stream of updates, bug reports, and immediate fixes and additions to the game to help with clarity.

As of posting this, there have been about 9 updates the help with clarity and bugs. Some may see this as a lack of playtesting. I see it as the devs being incredible accomodating and helpful. You can test a game for months, and still come out with bugs and issues that you didn't foresee because your testers just weren't indicative of EVERYONE playing the game. It happens. And these guys were prepared to handle any complaints. 

From the time I put the game down because of how I was stuck on the first Evidence Wave mission, to the time I picked it back up a day and a half later, major steps were taken to make even that mission in particular less brutally confusing. It's a walk in the park now, and a great introduction to the level style. 

All in all, this is more of a positive review of the devs than a positive review of the game. Because the game is phenomenal, and will continute to get better. The devs just happen to be...well, better than most that I've had to deal with.

I feel the game is quite a bit of fun but some of the negative reviews are correct in pointing out that instructions are sometimes less than clear.

On your first day of "work" (after getting hired) the mission briefing doesn't really explain specifically what you need to do.  I played the alpha and beta of this game and I can tell you that they actually did a better job of explaining this, not sure why they altered it.  Also they changed the assignment "rules" screen which used to be divided between suspicious people and suspicious data, now it just lists everything in a single list.  I personally liked it the old way but that may just be a subjective thing.

For those who are confused here are a few pointers to get you started:

1. On each suspects profile open their evidence which will be their web browsing history and/or their phone records.

2. If you find one of the names or websites in the assignment rules in those sections you need to:
   a) right click and select blacksheep tool
   b) select the relevant data (name or website)
   c) select the rule it relates to in the rules page
   d) mark the suspect as a "Threat" using the lightning (powers) button

3. If you find no evidence matching the rules, just click the powers button and select "Safe".

I don't know why the devs thought it would be a good idea to leave the above (or similar) instructions out of their game as it is bound to put people off, so yeah, I can understand some of the negatives so far.  But personally, I'm marking this as "recommended" because I'm enjoying it and I can say from playing the beta that the story gets more interesting as you get further into it.

Having said that, I really do hope the devs sort out this point of making things clearer to first time users.

review_text_raw: I got this game because I really loved Orwell and found it to be a thought provoking and thrilling story experience. This game, although comparable in premise, is definitely unique in its gameplay and purpose--you get prompted to "participate" (I say this loosely because your dialogue options are limited) in text/phone conversations as well as chats with your coworkers, and you can do "off the record" work from home. Like Papers, Please, more surveillance options open up as you play and there is an underlying plot. But I do have some issues with the mechanics of the game; as I mentioned before, dialogue options are very limited, and you're required to pursue certain paths in the story (you can't chose *not* to work for specific groups. You have to take all opportunities or you get a game over, which is kind of annoying). There's also some bugs and small annoying "Features"... The instructions/tutorials/exposition text all automatically progress (no "click to continue") so you can easily miss out on instructions or text. Sometimes the tutorial messages will get stuck and stop proceeding even though you've done what they've asked. Then it won't continue until you've gone ahead and figured out the tutorial section on your own. The game could use some more polish, but isn't unplayable and is fun enough.

review_text_raw:
I backed this game on Kickstarter 3 or 4 years ago and forgot about it till now. For 15 dollars (I paid 12), this game has been worth every penny. I really enjoyed the progression of security rankings and the data and power that came along with them. I also liked the ironic naming of the Department of Liberty. The little news headlines were interesting to read and paralleled our society in a way that made me think "Could this be us someday?" 

I don't know if your overall play style affects the endgame but I chose to play as a ruthless arm of the state just to see how far I could take my power. In the end, I chose to [spoiler] become the new director of the all powerful DoL and take down Charles Douglas. [/spoiler] However, in real life I found myself disgusted at the choices I "had" to make in the name of security and personal gain. Just knowing that I was violating privacy AND potentially ruining lives was quite the experience. The people I betrayed and killed felt real and conflicting. But alas, [strike] control [/strike] ... I mean security above all else, no?

The game can be played all through a mouse. A couple times my CODEX world-map background refused to pop up until I clicked it or tried to scroll. The biometric data was a little graphically glitchy. A few times I was confused at new task assignment types but I figured it out. Overall, a polished game with little complaints especially for how affordable it is. 

It felt rewarding to see Clearance Level 1, Rank = 1st. The soundtrack was [b] beautiful, [/b] truly well composed. The game made me feel conflict and emotion which is indicative of an excellent work of media/art/etc. If you are interested in surveillance, politics, culture, RPG's, or conflict this game is for you. After my play-through, I can't help to reflect on our own society and how much this game may or may not be representative of our current (and future) society. Excellent job Monomyth Games, kudos for this excellent game!

review_text_raw:
[h1]What is this game?[/h1]
It is the foremost NSA-watch-the-world-from-an-office simulator you will find as of the time of writing this review, and possibly for a long time.

You play a young man, joining a government agency. The rabbithole goes deep, and you are thrusted into a position of Orwellian surveillance, intrigue and thrill.

Starting at the bottom, you analyze simple things. Metadata, browser history and try to piece together a puzzle that is very clearly Need To Know. Given only slight glimpses of what is truly going on in this world. As you progress, you will advance in rank, getting a higher and higher level of clearance, and quickly find yourself face to face with the choice of whether or not to use your access for the good of the agency, the government, the country. the people or even yourself. 

Utilizing your powers of cyber-espionage to predict and even outright uncover your flings interests and hobbies, getting the IRS to get off your back, finding your sister/brother during an emergency or even getting out of paying your rent.

It very quickly becomes apparent what kind of power it actually is you are trusted with, and you will immediately realize why exactly it is so dangerous if left unchecked.

Don't just take it from me. Take it from the very person who knows this the best when he retweeted the game
[i]"Art imitates life."
~Edward Snowden[/i]

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The graphic artstyle of this game is great. It's minimalistic, but still detailed in the way it is done. The whole layout gives a sense of a point-and-click adventure, and for all intents and purposes it is.

Graphically, this game is unique in the way it focuses on the mechanics and uses the art direction to enhance them. You're never distracted by what's on the screen or in your peripheral vision, yet even after many hours (I'm writing this after a 24 hour bender on this game) it never ceases to be interesting or captivating. Artistically, it's very clear it was drawn by somebody who is passionate about the game, and it shows.

[h1]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h1]
The game had a very rough start at launch, with virtually no tutorial. That has been corrected. The team behind this game are very active both on the games own Subreddit, taking into account all the reports being thrown at them and have now rolled out the fourth daily patch in a row. Where else do you see that?

The gameplay itself is good. However, I will be the first to admit that it can be un-intuitive. The gameplay [b]does not change[/b], and thats strangely enough the charm and appeal.

Connect the dots as you chain together events from mere fragments of information such as e-mails, texts, social media, phone calls, browser history, bank account transcripts and decide the fate of the very people you've been spying on from behind your screen. Will you label them a threat for speaking their mind in, what they assumed to be total privacy and confidence, or will you stand up and become a whistleblower and help bring down this omniscient, omnipotent government entity?

Seemingly unrelated events tie together into something larger, and as you scale the ranks of this clandestine government, denying counter-surveillance groups information (or perhaps supplying it yourself), so does the plot thicken and grow.

I would most definitely recommend this game to pretty much anybody who likes a captivating experience.

It is not without flaws, but the developers have rolled out daily fixes since release, and are obviously very passionate about this game. It's not early access, but it isn't a triple-A polished and buffed product, either. But it is getting there.

Backed it on Kickstarter (I'm even in the credits if you looked!), played it, abandoned it for a few years, and then finally finished it, doesn't mean it's a boring game, hear me out.

Need to Know came from the era of Orwell - which I've also played, loved and reviewed - basically pattern matching gameplay laid on top of a "visual" novel (only without boobs). The gameplay, while has to be involved and brain-teasing, needs to tells a story.

Orwell excelled with being a more aggressively ramped-up authoritarian nightmare. A seemingly more far-fetched future. A story where an outsider can help control information, narratives, and through that, the truth and history.

(Mild spoilers ahead, skip next paragraph if you don't wanna know anything)

Need to Know, on the other hand, writes a story in a near future - where we may be right now, or in a few years. You play as a US citizen, whose sole power is to prosecute, to "just follow orders", and meanwhile trying to survive a personal political hell. You play yourself into becoming a regular crimer, a warcrimer, and a national terrorist. You see repercussion of your own actions in the story. You may justify yourself into believing you're fighting for "the truth"; yet the information you are given keeps getting worse, and it makes you wonder if you're becoming a eugenicist and a fascist. At that point, the only winning move may just be not to play, or yeet yourself into prison.

(Spoiler over)

If you choose to play on, the gameplay is more involved than Orwell - while Orwell only makes you marks single pieces of evidence, Need to Know makes you show the link between different pieces of seemingly unrelated information - only becoming related because you are given inside knowledge of what they may have been doing. Messages, tweets, locations, bank statements, satellite images, heartbeats - all the data we give willingly these days - can and will be used against them. You request more data, you use that data to find incriminating evidence, and you string them together to prosecute them. Everyday is like a mini-Sherlock Holmes mind palace minigame, only it keeps getting more complicated. It can get repetitive, but being engaged to the story and the new data types will help mitigate it a little bit.

The game represents a possible future, and you are a judge, jury, and executioner. Have fun doing war crimes.

Okay, so here we go. I've reached up to CL 3 now and have played the alpha version of this game as well. It's quite a bit of fun and I'm enjoying it.  PLEASE TRY THIS GAME. THE GRIND PAYS OFF.

Pros:
Neat concept, reasonably well executed by what I understand is a fairly novice indy team.
Developers are fixing the bugs
The art style is neat  (was kind of getting tired of Indy game meaning pixelart)
The CODEX facts are kinda funny sometimes and the little easteregg info bits are a nice touch.
The story is reasonably engaging
Fun sort of puzzle-type game
Doesn't feel like papers please
Hope to see new stuff get added in future as Devs are being fairly responsive to community input
The UI is well-optimized (especially when compared to the Beta)
Soundtrack isn't bad either.
The characters do actually feel like real people.
Cons

Sometimes the rules aren't always super clear and this can lead to some serious mission screwups (however, fret not, even if you get a huge compliance ding you can either A) exit the mission before going home (this will restart it from the login screen or B) Just eat the compliance hit because usually the next mission is more forgiving it's usually a couple easy missions then a kind of tough one and then a few easier ones)

The missions can feel a little grind-y. 

There's some stuff missing that seems like it should be there (There's no stock trading system as promised, the shop only has a handfull of items to buy, no cars or anything like what was in the original trailer for this game).

The first couple CLs are a grind. I've got almost 17 hours into the game and I'm at CL 3 (you start at 10). The real fun doesn't really start until about CL 6 or so and I think that's pushing a couple people away from the game.

The Data selling thing is just kind of super annoying and stretches the gameplay out unnecessarily while adding little to the story.

Wish there were more character customization options. 


TL;DR: Neat indy game, responsive development team. Can be a little grind-y through the first bit but gets pretty good after that.

EDIT: After playing an additional 14 hours, I felt it was best to revise my original review. I can rate this game as being recommended, so long as you're okay with a few necessary compromises. I'll explain those below.

I wanted to like this game very badly, but 5 hours in and I'm starting to see the seams and cracks that make this a less than perfect experience. I think my dissatisfaction with the gameplay comes down to one question: when you played Papers, Please, was your favorite part of the game the times where you had to squint at the IDs to see if that was a D or a P or a G? If so, you'll love this game. Everyone else will be irritated, and rightfully so.

The game is beautiful - I loved the interface and the art style. The story, at least so far, is passable and engaging, and I'm conflicted about finishing the game because of its flaws and the main reason is because I do want to see how the story resolves itself, and there's an early "flash-forward" that has me intrigued about what remains to be experienced.

But when the core gameplay is "spot the difference between two letters or numbers" or "try to remember this ridiculously complex flow chart of rules and protocols", it gets exhausting. It also doesn't help that for me, the game was slow and plodding at times. Opening up a menu sometimes took 2 or 3 seconds longer than you expected it to, and visual transitions sometimes slowed to a crawl. Add to that the completely boring gameplay loops and you have a recipe for boredom.

So again, to summarize... if you have fun deciding which of these three names - P Vasquez and D Vasqez and B Vaskez - matches the one in a briefing supplied to you before the stage begins, and you can suspend your disbelief that so many people would have more than one variation of the same name in their address books, then you'll like the game. Otherwise, maybe read a plot summary.

UPDATE: I stuck with the game because of the story, as I mentioned. And I was surprised to see - well into the game - that the gameplay does get mixed up in interesting ways eventually. There are still lots of repetitive tasks that seem to be there just because, at the end of the day, this is a game and not a true simulation. But there was something to the premise and the characterization and dialogue that kept me wanting to press forward even when it was monotonous. If you think you're up for the task and have nearly 20 hours to spare, the ending is passable.

This game is not without it's problems, but for it's price, and the assumption that the problems will be fixed, I personally think it's worth a playthrough, especially if commentary on Orwellian government is something that interests you. Having finished the game once, I'm unsure if there are points of divergence in the story, but I do know there are conditions where
you fail and have to restart, and there are in fact multiple endings.

Pros:
-Engaging storyline.
-Pretty interface, actually makes you feel like you're sitting in an office doing this stuff.
-Simple, easy to follow gameplay, most of the time.
-Lots of different actions you can take make it feel like you're doing different things even though you aren't really.
-The mission where you interrogate the guy was REALLY fun and I wish they had more of those.

Cons:
-Gameplay can be frustrating at times, particularly on a certain mission type where it's unclear which power you are meant to use to Discard/Ignore/NoMatch people, and using the wrong power makes you lose compliance.
-Minor spelling errors littered throughout the game.
-Certain parts ("post-mission missions") can be really boring, but they are fast and even skippable.
-Certain bugs, but nothing gamebreaking. For instance, there was one case of 3 pieces of evidence having to be linked, but you can only link 2 at once.
-Clarity on which tool to use could be better, but that's more my fault on not paying attention.
-Interface clunky at times.

Overall, I'd say 6.5/10. This game, like I said, is not without it's flaws, but they can be corrected, and if you like the concept and you liked Papers Please, you'll have a fun time with this. The pros do outweigh the cons, though it can be a bit of a slog to get through sometimes and it can be a bit frustrating. At the end of the day, for 15 bucks, it's worth a playthrough.

I loved this game. Recommend.

Selling point:
The morally ambigious writing and the logical characters. The game makes you feel you are part of a 90s political thriller, set in the modern world.

Pros:
- writing is amazing
- puzzles are logical and set in the real world
- aesthetics are minimalistic, but cool (my only gripe is that some people looked bizarre),
- game duration (game changes pace once it gets slightly repetitive, which was welcome)
- world-building (despite its conspiracy context, the game is very much grounded in the real world both in terms of politics and technology, and everything felt contemporary, even in its future years)
- achievements (100% completion is based on completing the game, not on some wild goose chase)

Cons:
- UI (common visual glitches, although I do play on linux which may add glitches; animations are slow, changing suspects is slow, link puzzles between multiple suspects are slow not due to complexity of puzzle but due to UI problems; clicking on suspects is difficult even if you remove map scrolling)
- some puzzle solutions have obtuse or small consequences, could have kept its linearity but with some more impact on world, you do get some comics balloons for some optional objectives
- game does push you to become a government bot, even if your character disagrees wildly with that (but this is somewhat necessary from a writing standpoint).

In Brief:
This is a very good game for someone who is interested in mass surveillance, abuse of power, corporate capitalism, world politics, solving puzzles, and in general feeling like a special part of an important conspiracy.

This game was definitely cool - a more drawn-out, involved and far-reaching Papers Please - but one major thing needs to be mentioned. It feels like it was written by a librarian. What I mean is that everything must be clicked in PRECISELY the right way, in EXACTLY the right order. If you have three tools at your disposal, you must use them in EXACTLY the way the developers intended - often with missing or contradictory instructions as to how to do that. 

I still recommend this game, though, because if you can navigate the steep learning curve, it's fun and interesting. Even if maybe a trifle too real in this day and age.

The game had a few, in my opinion minor, flaws at the start but it's still fun. I enjoy the fact that this game actually makes me think and look for little details. I was confused by the lack of tutorial but I managed to figure things out and I am glad to see they have since added one in. The devs are releasing daily fixes and seem to be staying on top of things and actually listening to feedback. 

TL;DR: Game was pretty good; Devs making constant improvents: now game is better.

review_text_raw: Enjoyable game,  great if you enjoy point and click format. I like the high stakes that the storyline provides. However, at times, the mission instructions can be a bit vague, which can affect your character's analysis accuracy.  I also don't like the game narrative forces the player to sell intelligence to parties that aren't a part of the game's government structure, which essentially places the player in the position of selling classified information to the highest bidder.
